title: Custom metadata types, custom settings, custom labels, and named credentials overview
objectives: Choose custom metadata types when configuration records should deploy and package as metadata.
Explain list versus hierarchy custom settings as cached configuration data, and why unprotected settings are a poor secret store.
Use custom labels for translatable UI text, not for endpoints or passwords.
Use named credentials (and external credentials) for callout endpoints and authentication, not for ordinary app mappings.
diagnostic_question: A package needs deployable discount rates, a per-user debug flag, a translated error string, and an authenticated callout to a vendor API. Which of custom metadata types, custom settings, custom labels, and named credentials do you use for each—and where do you refuse to put the password?
definition: Custom metadata types store deployable, packageable configuration as metadata records. Custom settings are similar to custom objects but cached: list settings are org-wide static data; hierarchy settings personalize by organization, profile, then user. Custom labels store translatable text. A named credential specifies a callout endpoint and authentication in one definition; Winter '23 introduced preferred named credentials paired with external credentials, and legacy named credentials are deprecated. Do not store secrets in ordinary custom settings. ([Custom Settings](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_customsettings.htm); [Get Started with Named Credentials](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/named-credentials/guide/get-started.html); [Storing Sensitive Data](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.secure_coding_guide.meta/secure_coding_guide/secure_coding_storing_sensitive_data.htm); [Custom Metadata Types](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.custommetadatatypes_about.htm))
why_it_matters: Interviewers listen for metadata versus data. Custom setting rows are data (definitions package, data does not). Custom metadata records travel with the deployment. Named credentials are the callout secret surface. Putting an OAuth token in a public custom setting is a Secure Coding fail—Help and the Apex guide warn that unprotected settings are readable, including by the guest user.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of airport operations. Custom metadata types are the published flight schedule that deploys with the airline—configuration that should move between orgs. Custom settings are the cached gate board: list settings are the same for everyone; hierarchy settings can override at profile or user. Custom labels are the multilingual PA announcements. Named credentials are the jetway badge: endpoint plus authentication, not a discount-rate table. Do not tape the badge PIN to the public gate board.
deeper_explanation: Custom settings: developers create data sets for the org, profile, or user. Data is in the application cache for efficient access without repeated SOQL. Formula fields, validation rules, flows, Apex, and SOAP API can use them. List settings are org-wide static data. Hierarchy settings return the most specific value: user overrides profile overrides organization. Only the custom setting definition packages, not the data; populate after install. Apex tests treat existing custom settings as data and need SeeAllData=true to see them—or create them in test setup. ([Custom Settings](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_customsettings.htm))

Protection: only custom settings marked protected and installed in a managed package are protected. Otherwise they are treated as public and readable for all profiles, including the guest user. Do not store secrets, PII, or private data there. Outside a managed package, use named credentials or encrypted custom fields for secrets. ([Custom Settings](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_customsettings.htm); [Storing Sensitive Data](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.secure_coding_guide.meta/secure_coding_guide/secure_coding_storing_sensitive_data.htm))

Custom metadata types: configuration records that deploy and package as metadata, unlike custom setting data. Use them for mappings and rules that must move between sandboxes. Protected CMT in a managed package can hold package secrets readable from same-namespace Apex. Subscriber-org CMT is not a hiding place for tokens. ([Storing Sensitive Data](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.secure_coding_guide.meta/secure_coding_guide/secure_coding_storing_sensitive_data.htm); [Custom Metadata Types](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.custommetadatatypes_about.htm))

Named credentials specify the callout URL and authentication. Preferred pattern: named credential (endpoint/transport) plus external credential (protocol and principals). Legacy named credentials are deprecated and will be discontinued. Users with Customize Application can view named credentials; if policy requires hiding secrets from subscribers, use protected CMT or protected custom settings in a managed package instead. ([Get Started](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/named-credentials/guide/get-started.html); [Storing Sensitive Data](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.secure_coding_guide.meta/secure_coding_guide/secure_coding_storing_sensitive_data.htm))

Custom labels are translatable UI strings (error text, button labels). They are metadata, not a configuration table and not a credential store. Exact Help article IDs for labels are neighboring—treat labels as official Setup metadata and do not store endpoints in them.

mental_model.analogy: Airport operations: custom metadata is the published flight schedule that deploys with the airline, custom settings are the cached gate board (list vs hierarchy overrides), custom labels are multilingual PA announcements, and named credentials are the jetway badge.
useful_mapping: custom metadata type + records → published schedule that deploys
list custom setting → org-wide cached board
hierarchy custom setting → user/profile/org override on the board
custom label → PA announcement in each language
external credential → the badge protocol and who may use it
public custom setting secret → PIN taped to the public board
where_it_breaks: Hierarchy getInstance() details are more specific than a paper board.
Legacy versus new named credentials is a platform deprecation, not an airport rule.
Protected package secrets are a namespace story the PA system does not show.
Custom labels are not error-message location (DATA-010) even if you store the text there.

claims.claim: Only the custom setting definition is included in packages, not the data. Protection applies only to protected settings in a managed package; otherwise settings are public and readable, including by the guest user. Do not store secrets there.
claims.validation: Apex guide warning plus Secure Coding Guide.

claims.claim: A named credential specifies a callout endpoint and authentication. Prefer named credentials plus external credentials; legacy named credentials are deprecated. Named credentials are for callout auth, not arbitrary secrets if Customize Application users must not see them.
claims.validation: Named Credentials Get Started plus Secure Coding Guide.

claims.claim: Custom metadata types hold deployable, packageable configuration metadata. Protected CMT in a managed package can store package-wide secrets for same-namespace Apex. Use custom labels for translatable text, not endpoints or passwords.

terminology.precise: A type whose records are metadata: customizable, deployable, packageable application configuration.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Custom object used as config: data, not metadata, unless you migrate.
terminology.boundary: Protected packaged CMT is a secret pattern for ISVs.

terminology.plain: Cached configuration similar to a custom object.
terminology.precise: List or hierarchy data in the application cache; usable from formulas, validation, Flow, Apex, and SOAP API.
terminology.non_example: A normal custom object queried every time with SOQL.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: CMT: deployable records vs setting data.

terminology.precise: Static data that does not vary by profile or user, such as country codes. Cached so you avoid repeated SOQL.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Custom metadata list of rates that must deploy: prefer CMT.
terminology.boundary: Still not for secrets if public.

terminology.plain: Org, then profile, then user override.
terminology.precise: Returns the most specific, lowest value. getInstance() reads that hierarchy.
terminology.example: Debug_Enabled__c true for one user, false at org.
terminology.non_example: A list setting of country codes.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Profile assignment of page layouts: different feature.
terminology.boundary: Create test data in tests; do not rely on org data.

terminology.precise: Metadata strings for messages and labels, not endpoints or passwords.
terminology.example: Error_Enter_Region custom label used by a validation message or LWC.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Validation error message typed only in one language on the rule.

terminology.precise: Specifies the URL and HTTP transport; pair with an external credential in the preferred model. Legacy named credentials are deprecated.
terminology.non_example: A custom label holding a password.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Remote site setting: older endpoint allow-list, neighboring.
terminology.boundary: Customize Application users can view them.

terminology.precise: Used by one or more named credentials; maps principals to permissions; stores encrypted tokens as user external credentials.
terminology.example: OAuth external credential reused by two named credentials.
terminology.non_example: A list custom setting of tokens.

terminology.plain: Secrets only in protected managed-package CMT or settings.
terminology.precise: Secure Coding: protected CMT or protected custom settings inside a managed package. Public settings are readable, including by guest users.
terminology.example: Managed package API key in protected CMT.
terminology.non_example: Token in an unprotected hierarchy setting in the subscriber org.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Encrypted custom field: another allowed pattern the Apex guide mentions outside packages.
terminology.boundary: Never tape the PIN to the public board.

when_to_use: When configuration records must deploy or package as metadata—use a custom metadata type.
When you need cached org-wide list data or hierarchy overrides by profile or user—use custom settings.
When UI text must be translated—use a custom label.
When Apex or automation must call an external HTTP endpoint with authentication—use a named credential (preferred: plus external credential).
When explaining why a public custom setting is the wrong place for a password or token.
when_not_to_use: Do not store OAuth tokens or passwords in ordinary/public custom settings or custom labels.
Do not use a named credential as a general discount-rate or mapping table.
Do not use a custom setting when the rows must deploy between sandboxes—use CMT.
Do not use CMT or settings as a substitute for ordinary business objects, fields, or relationships (DATA-001–004).
Do not use hierarchy settings as a security model in place of profiles and sharing.
configuration_or_code_location: Setup → Custom Metadata Types; Custom Settings; Custom Labels; Named Credentials.
Apex: custom setting getInstance/getAll; CMT SOQL; callout:NamedCredential.
Formulas and validation can reference custom settings (and some CMT—confirm current formula support).
Packaging: setting definition only; CMT records included as metadata.

interview_questions.question: Compare custom metadata types and custom settings.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: CMT records are metadata that deploy and package. Custom settings are cached data: list or hierarchy. Only the setting definition packages, not the rows. Both can hold configuration; they differ in deploy and hierarchy.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I use CMT for rates that must move between orgs. I use hierarchy settings for per-user flags. I warn that public settings are guest-readable. I do not use either as Account storage. I mention Apex tests isolate setting data.
interview_questions.example: LAB_SeverityMap__mdt deploys; LAB_UserFlags__c rows do not.

interview_questions.question: Where do you put a vendor API password?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: In a named credential / external credential for a callout. Not in a public custom setting, custom label, or Apex constant. ISV package-wide keys use protected packaged CMT or settings.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I cite Custom Settings and Secure Coding. Customize Application users can view named credentials, so subscriber-hidden secrets use protected packaged configuration. I prefer the new NC model. I never log the token.
interview_questions.example: callout:LAB_VendorNC with an external credential; no Password__c on a setting.
follow_ups: Who can see the named credential?
What is an external credential principal?
weak_answer_warnings: Putting the password in a list setting

interview_questions.question: Per-user debug flag. Which tool?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: A hierarchy custom setting so user overrides profile overrides org. Not a named credential and not a CMT row per user as the first design.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I set org default false and enable one LAB_ user. Apex uses getInstance(). Tests create the setting. If the flag must deploy per user, that is a strange requirement—I would question it. I do not store a token next to the flag.
interview_questions.example: LAB_UserFlags__c.Debug__c true only for the tester.
follow_ups: Does getInstance() without a user use the running user?
Can validation rules read the flag?
weak_answer_warnings: A CMT record named after each user

interview_questions.question: What is a custom label for, and what is it not for?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Translatable UI strings such as error text. Not endpoints, not passwords, not discount tables.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I may point a validation message or LWC at a label for Translation Workbench. I still write actionable message text (DATA-010). I do not hide a named credential URL in a label. I mark Workbench steps neighboring if asked for click-path.
interview_questions.example: Label Error_Enter_Region used by a rule or component.
follow_ups: How do you translate a label?
weak_answer_warnings: Storing a refresh token in a label

interview_questions.question: The package installed but country-code rows are missing.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: You packaged a custom setting. Only the definition travels. Load the rows after install or switch deployable rows to a custom metadata type.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I check whether the component was a setting or CMT. I do not tell the subscriber the package is corrupt. I add a post-install script only if we stay on settings—and I remember that is extra work CMT avoids. I do not put secrets in those missing rows.
interview_questions.example: Change set had LAB_CountryCode__c definition and zero rows; CMT would have included records.
follow_ups: Do unlocked packages include CMT records?
Can you include setting data somehow?

interview_questions.question: Apex test fails to read the org's hierarchy setting.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Tests isolate data. Create the custom setting in test setup. SeeAllData=true sees org settings but is a last resort the guide discourages as a best practice.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I write a @TestSetup method that inserts the hierarchy row. I do not depend on a sandbox admin's leftover data. I mention the guide's SeeAllData note so the interviewer hears I read it. I still do not store secrets in that test row.
interview_questions.example: Test creates LAB_UserFlags__c org default without SeeAllData.
follow_ups: Do CMT records need the same treatment?
What about SeeAllData in a managed package test?
weak_answer_warnings: Turning on SeeAllData as the first fix always

interview_questions.question: Legacy named credential versus named plus external credential?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Prefer the newer named credential plus external credential. Legacy named credentials are deprecated and will be discontinued. I would not design a new integration on legacy.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I explain endpoint/transport versus protocol/principals. One external credential can serve several named credentials. I reverify the current deprecation notice rather than quoting a retirement date. I still would not put the password in a setting while we migrate.
interview_questions.example: New LAB_ vendor callout uses NC + external credential; old legacy NC is on a migration list.
tradeoffs: Reuse external credential vs one legacy NC each
weak_answer_warnings: Starting a new project on legacy NC

interview_questions.question: How do these four tools differ from objects, fields, and relationships?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Objects and fields store business records (DATA-001–004). These four store configuration, text, or callout identity. Using a custom object as a config table is data you must migrate; CMT is metadata you deploy.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I keep the handbook split: schema versus configuration. I mention settings can be read from formulas and validation, so they sit next to DATA-006/010, but they are not a substitute for typed fields on Property. I refuse to model Accounts as CMT.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Property__c remains an object; LAB_SeverityMap__mdt is configuration.
tradeoffs: Custom object as config vs CMT
follow_ups: When is a custom object still the right config UI?
weak_answer_warnings: Putting customer properties in a custom setting
